nodes.name: Bernstein block
nodes.statement:
In \cite{Bernstein1984}, J.~Bernstein gives a decomposition of the category of smooth 
representations of $G$ into indecomposable full subcategories, called \emph{blocks}, that are indexed
by the inertial support of the irreducible representations they contain.

nodes.name: Type (for a supercuspidal representation)
nodes.statement:
Given an irreducible supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$, a \emph{type} for $\pi$ is a pair $(K, \lambda)$ consisting of an
irreducible representation $\lambda$ of a compact open subgroup $K$ of $G$ such that $\mathrm{Ind}_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$.
differentia: $\mathrm{Ind}_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$

nodes.name: Representation containing a type
nodes.statement: In this case, $\lambda$ occurs as a subrepresentation of $\pi|_K$ and we say $\pi$ \emph{contains} the type $(K,\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Existence of types for essentially tame supercuspidals (Adler, Yu, Kim)
nodes.statement:
In particular, the work of J.~Adler \cite{Adler1998}, generalized by J.K.~Yu \cite{Yu2001}, shows that every essentially tame
supercuspidal representation contains a type; the work of J.-L.~Kim \cite{Kim2007} assures us that if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large, then all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form.
nodes.statement_short: Every essentially tame supercuspidal contains a type (Adler, Yu); for $p$ large all supercuspidals are essentially tame (Kim).
assumptions: if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large
conclusions:
every essentially tame
supercuspidal representation contains a type
all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form

nodes.name: Conjugates and inductions of types are types
nodes.statement:
Given a supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$, it is simple to
produce additional types: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type, as
is any pair $(K', \tau)$ where $K'$ is a compact open subgroup of $G$ containing $K$ and $\tau$ is
an irreducible representation of $K'$ that contains $\lambda$ upon restriction to $K$.
assumptions: $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$
conclusions: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type
nodes.statement_short: G-conjugates of a type, and irreducible reps of larger compact open subgroups containing it, are again types.

nodes.name: Unicity of types
nodes.statement:
A natural
question to ask is whether $\pi$ can contain any additional types, specifically on \emph{maximal} compact open subgroups, that are not related to $(K,\lambda)$ in this way.  It is expected that this should never happen, and the conjecture that
this is the case is known as the \emph{unicity of types}.
nodes.statement_short: Every type of $\pi$ on a maximal compact open subgroup arises, up to conjugacy, from the given type by conjugation and induction.

nodes.name: Known cases of the unicity conjecture
nodes.statement: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ \cite{Latham2016}, for essentially tame representations of $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$ \cite{Latham2018}, and for depth-zero supercuspidal representations of any connected reductive $p$-adic group $G$ \cite{Latham2017}.
conclusions: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ \cite{Latham2016}, for essentially tame representations of $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$ \cite{Latham2018}, and for depth-zero supercuspidal representations of any connected reductive $p$-adic group $G$ \cite{Latham2017}

nodes.name: Strong unicity property
nodes.statement:
In each of these cases, it was seen that a stronger property holds, namely,  that if $K\subset G$ is any maximal compact open subgroup,
then there exists, up to $G$-conjugacy, at most one type defined on $K$ for each supercuspidal
representation $\pi$ of $G$.  We will refer to this as the \emph{strong unicity property}.
nodes.statement_short: For every maximal compact open $K$, $\pi$ has at most one type on $K$ up to $G$-conjugacy.
also_stated_at: Recall that strong unicity of types is the statement that $\mathrm{Res}_{K}\pi$ should contain at most one type, for each choice of maximal compact open subgroup $K$.

nodes.name: G simply connected semisimple
nodes.statement: From now on, let us specialize to the case that $G$ is a simply connected semisimple $p$-adic group.

nodes.name: Toral supercuspidal representation
nodes.statement:
We restrict our attention here to  those sequences for which the smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic (also called elliptic) maximal torus of $G$.    
For the purposes of this paper we call these \emph{toral} supercuspidal representations, though we caution the reader that some authors reserve ``toral'' to mean the more restrictive case that the twisted Levi sequence has length $d=1$.
differentia: the smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic (also called elliptic) maximal torus of $G$

nodes.name: Branching rules of supercuspidals to maximal compacts
nodes.statement:
The restriction of $\pi$ to a maximal compact open subgroup $G_y$ 
  decomposes as an infinite direct sum of irreducible representations of $G_y$.  Describing these branching rules is a difficult open problem of interest in its own right.

nodes.name: Types on G_y are the components not shared with other representations
nodes.statement: Here, it suffices to note that with $G$ as above, the Bernstein block corresponding to $\pi$ is generated by $\pi$.  Therefore the types of $\pi$ supported on $G_y$ are exactly those irreducible components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ that do not occur in $\pi'|_{G_y}$ for any other (inequivalent) irreducible representation $\pi'$ of $G$.
conclusions: the types of $\pi$ supported on $G_y$ are exactly those irreducible components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ that do not occur in $\pi'|_{G_y}$ for any other (inequivalent) irreducible representation $\pi'$ of $G$
assumptions: with $G$ as above
nodes.statement_short: Since $\pi$ generates its Bernstein block, types on $G_y$ are the components of $\pi|_{G_y}$ not occurring in any other irreducible $\pi'|_{G_y}$.

nodes.name: Main theorem (unicity of types for toral supercuspidal representations)
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$ and suppose $\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$.  If the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$, then $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.   Moreover, in this case, $\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\mathcal{B}^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\mathcal{B}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: If depth of $\phi_0$ exceeds $2c_T$, $\pi$ satisfies unicity of types; strong unicity holds iff $\mathcal{B}^T$ is the closure of a single facet.
assumptions: $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$
$\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$
the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$
conclusions: $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$
$\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\mathcal{B}^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\mathcal{B}(G)$
equivalent_conditions: $\mathcal{B}^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\mathcal{B}(G)$

nodes.name: Small-depth case and general twisted Levi sequences
nodes.statement: Several interesting problems remain open.  The hypothesis on the depth of the character of $T$ given in the statement of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity} arises as a result of our method of proof.  There is no such restriction for the unicity theorems on $G=\mathrm{GL}_n$ or on $G=\mathrm{SL}_n$, where a different argument (particular to type A) was employed by V.~Pa\u{s}k\={u}nas to address the small-depth case.  Finally, not all essentially tame supercuspidal representations arise from toral data; the consideration of general twisted Levi sequences is necessary to completely resolve the unicity conjecture in these cases.
nodes.statement_short: Open: remove the depth hypothesis, and treat supercuspidals from non-toral twisted Levi sequences.

nodes.name: Local field F
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a nonarchimedean local field of residual characteristic $p$, with integer ring ${\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Normalized valuation
nodes.statement:
We normalize the valuation 
$
u$ on $F$ so that $
u(F^	imes) =\mathbb{Z}$; if $E$ is an extension field of $F$ then we also denote by $
u$ the unique extension of this valuation to $E$.

nodes.name: Additive character Lambda
nodes.statement: Fix an additive character $\Lambda$ of $F$ that is nontrivial on ${\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}$ but trivial on $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Conjugate subgroup and representation
nodes.statement: If $H\subset G$ are groups and $g\in G$, let ${}^gH = \{ghg^{-1}\mid h\in H\}$ and for any representation $\tau$ of $H$ let ${}^g\tau$ denote the corresponding representation of ${}^gH$.

nodes.name: Restriction notation
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is a representation of $G$ we write $\mathrm{Res}_H\sigma$ for its restriction to $H$.

nodes.name: The group G
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a semisimple simply connected linear algebraic group defined over $F$ and let $G = \mathbf{G}(F)$.

nodes.name: Reduced building B(G)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{B}(G)=\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ denote the reduced building of $\mathbf{G}$ over $F$; since $\mathbf{G}$ is semisimple it coincides with the enlarged building.

nodes.name: Point stabilizers are parahoric
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbf{G}$ is simply connected, the stabilizer of a point $x$ in the building, $G_x$, coincides with the parahoric subgroup $G_{x,0}$ associated to the facet containing $x$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{G}$ is simply connected
conclusions: the stabilizer of a point $x$ in the building, $G_x$, coincides with the parahoric subgroup $G_{x,0}$ associated to the facet containing $x$

nodes.name: Maximal compact open subgroups are vertex stabilizers
nodes.statement: Both hypotheses together imply that the maximal compact open subgroups of $G$ are exactly the maximal parahoric subgroups of $G$, that is, $G_y$ for each vertex $y$ of the building.
assumptions: Both hypotheses together
conclusions: the maximal compact open subgroups of $G$ are exactly the maximal parahoric subgroups of $G$, that is, $G_y$ for each vertex $y$ of the building

nodes.name: Maximal split torus S
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{S}$ be a maximal $F$-split torus in $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.

nodes.name: Maximal unramified-split torus S'
nodes.statement: Fix a maximal unramified extension $F^{un}$ of $F$, and let $\mathbf{S}'$ be a maximal $F^{un}$-split torus of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$ and containing $\mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: Centralizer torus Z
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{Z}$ be the centralizer of $\mathbf{S}'$ in $\mathbf{G}$, which is a maximal torus of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.

nodes.name: Root system and apartment
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Phi = \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})$ the root system of $\mathbf{G}$ relative to $\mathbf{S}$ and by ${\mathcal{A}} = {\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S}, F)$ the apartment of $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ corresponding to $\mathbf{S}$.

nodes.name: Affine roots
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi_\Phi$ be the set of affine roots, corresponding to our choice of valuation $\nu$; these are functions on ${\mathcal{A}}$.

nodes.name: Root subgroup
nodes.statement: Denote the root subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ corresponding to $\alpha \in \Phi$ by $\mathbf{G}_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Filtration of root subgroups
nodes.statement: For $\alpha \in \Phi$ we set $G_\alpha=\mathbf{G}_{\alpha}(F)$; this group admits a filtration by compact open subgroups $G_\psi$, as $\psi$ runs over the affine roots with gradient $\dot\psi=\alpha$.

nodes.name: F-points S, S', Z
nodes.statement: Let $S=\mathbf{S}(F)$, $S'=\mathbf{S}'(F)$ and $Z=\mathbf{Z}(F)$.

nodes.name: Maximal bounded subgroup of Z
nodes.statement: Let $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ be the maximal bounded subgroup of $Z$.

nodes.name: Filtration of a torus
nodes.statement: Recall that any torus $T=\mathbf{T}(F)$ admits a natural filtration by subgroups $T_r$ for $r\geq 0$, and its Lie algebra $\mathfrak{t}$ is filtered by lattices $\mathfrak{t}_r$ for $r\in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Filtration of Z
nodes.statement: In particular, $Z$ admits a natural filtration by subgroups $Z_{r}$ for $r\geq 0$, with $Z_0\subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad filtration subgroups
nodes.statement:
For any $x\in {\mathcal{A}}$ and $r\geq 0$, A.~Moy and G.~Prasad \cite{MoyPrasad1994} defined $G_{\alpha,x,r} = \langle G_\psi \mid \psi(x)\geq r, \dot\psi=\alpha \rangle$ and thus filtration subgroups
 $$
 G_{x,r}=\langle Z_{r}, G_{\alpha,x,r} \mid \alpha \in \Phi\rangle 
  $$
  of $G_x$.
nodes.statement_short: Moy-Prasad filtration subgroups $G_{x,r}$ generated by $Z_r$ and root subgroups $G_\psi$ with $\psi(x)\ge r$.

nodes.name: G_{x,r+}
nodes.statement: We set $G_{x,r+} = \cup_{s>r}G_{x,s}$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad lattices
nodes.statement: They similarly defined lattices $\mathfrak{g}_{x,r}$ in $\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Lie}(G)(F)$ and $\mathfrak{g}^*_{x,r}$ in  $\mathfrak{g}^*$, indexed by $r\in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: We say that a group $\mathbf{G}'$ (or its set of $F$-points $G' = \mathbf{G}'(F)$) is a \emph{twisted Levi subgroup} of $\mathbf{G}$ if there is an extension $E$ of $F$ such that  $\mathbf{G}'$ is an $E$-Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$.
differentia: there is an extension $E$ of $F$ such that  $\mathbf{G}'$ is an $E$-Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ defined over $F$

nodes.name: Tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: We say $\mathbf{G}'$ is tamely ramified if $\mathbf{G}'$ (and thus $\mathbf{G}$) splits over a tamely ramified extension.

nodes.name: Twisted Levi G', torus T, splitting field E
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $\mathbf{G}'$ is a (tamely ramified) twisted Levi subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ and let $\mathbf{T}$ be a maximal torus of $\mathbf{G}'$; let $E$ be a tamely ramified splitting field of $\mathbf{T}$ over $F$.

nodes.name: Lie algebra of G' and dual of its center
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{g}'$ denote the $F$-points of $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}')$, and denote by ${\mathfrak{z}'}^*$ the $F$-points of the dual of the center of $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}')$.

nodes.name: G-generic element of depth -r
nodes.statement: Let $r>0$.  Following \cite[Definition 3.7]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^*_{-r}$ is called \emph{$G$-generic of depth $-r$} if it satisfies the conditions \textbf{GE1} and \textbf{GE2} of \cite[\S8]{Yu2001}.
differentia: it satisfies the conditions \textbf{GE1} and \textbf{GE2} of \cite[\S8]{Yu2001}

nodes.name: Yu's Lemma 8.1 (genericity conditions)
nodes.statement: By \cite[Lemma 8.1]{Yu2001}, if $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})$, then these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})\setminus\Phi(\mathbf{G}',\mathbf{T})$, where $H_a \in \mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G})(E)$ is the coroot associated to $a$.
assumptions: $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})$
conclusions: these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{T})\setminus\Phi(\mathbf{G}',\mathbf{T})$
nodes.statement_short: For $p$ not a torsion prime, genericity of $X^*$ reduces to $\nu(\langle X^*,H_a\rangle)=-r$ for roots outside $G'$.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad isomorphism
nodes.statement:
Fix also a Moy-Prasad isomorphism \cite[\S 2.6]{HakimMurnaghan2008}
$$
e \colon G'_{x,r}/G'_{x,r+} \to \mathfrak{g}'_{x,r}/\mathfrak{g}'_{x,r+}.
$$

nodes.name: Character realized by an element
nodes.statement:
A character $\phi$ of $G'$ of depth $r$ is said to be \emph{realized by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ on $G'_{x,r}$} if 
for every $Y \in \mathfrak{g}'_{x,r}$, 
$$
\phi(e(Y+\mathfrak{g}'_{x,r+})) = \Lambda(\langle X^*, Y\rangle).
$$

nodes.name: G-generic character
nodes.statement: By \cite[Definition 3.9]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, $\phi$ is \emph{$G$-generic (relative to $x$) of depth $r>0$} if $\phi$ is trivial on $G'_{x,r+}$, nontrivial on $G'_{x,r}$, and is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$.
differentia: is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mathfrak{z}'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$

nodes.name: Yu's Lemma 8.3 (generic characters and conjugation)
nodes.statement: A particular consequence of the $G$-genericity of a character $\phi$ of $G'$ is that for any $g\in G$, we have that ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$ \cite[Lemma 8.3]{Yu2001}.
assumptions: $G$-genericity of a character $\phi$ of $G'$
for any $g\in G$
conclusions: ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$

nodes.name: Toral supercuspidal datum
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.definiendum: positive-depth generic toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$
differentia: $\vec{G} = (G^0\subsetneq G^1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq G^d=G)$, for some $d \geq 1$, is a sequence of tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroups, such that in particular $G^0=T$ an anisotropic maximal torus in $G$
$\vec{\phi} = (\phi_0, \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{d-1})$ where $\phi_i$ is a $G^{i+1}$-generic character of $G^i$ of depth $r_i$, and these real numbers satisfy $0<r_0<r_1 < \cdots < r_{d-1}$
nodes.statement_short: A pair of a tame twisted Levi sequence starting at an anisotropic torus $T$ and generic characters $\phi_i$ of increasing depths $r_i$.

nodes.name: Half-depths s_i
nodes.statement: For convenience we write $s_i = r_i/2$ for each $i = 0, \ldots, d-1$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Point x of B(T) in B(G)
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is anisotropic, the image of $\mathcal{B}(T)$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$ consists of a single point $x$, and it is this point relative to which the characters $\phi_i$ are $G^{i+1}$-generic.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: K^0
nodes.statement: Set $\mathsf{K}^0=G^0_x=T$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Inducing subgroups K^i
nodes.statement:
For each $1\leq i\leq d$ define  
$$
\mathsf{K}^i:= G^0_{x}G^1_{x,s_0}\cdots G^{i}_{x,s_{i-1}} 
\subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_x.
$$

nodes.name: Properties of the subgroups J^i
nodes.statement: The groups in these products have large pairwise intersections, so we next define subgroups $\mathsf{J}^i$ and $\mathsf{J}^i_+$ which will have the property that $\mathsf{K}^i\mathsf{J}^{i+1}=\mathsf{K}^{i+1}$ and $\mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1} = \mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ = G^i_{x,r_i}$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: $\mathsf{K}^i\mathsf{J}^{i+1}=\mathsf{K}^{i+1}$
$\mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1} = \mathsf{K}^i\cap \mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ = G^i_{x,r_i}$

nodes.name: Splitting field E of T
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a tamely ramified Galois extension of $F$ over which $\mathbf{T}$ splits.

nodes.name: Root systems Phi_i
nodes.statement: For each $0\leq i\leq d$, let $\Phi_i = \Phi(\mathbf{G}^i,\mathbf{T})$ be the corresponding root system.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Group J(E)^{i+1}
nodes.statement:
For $0 \leq i < d$ let $\mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}$ be the group generated by $\mathbf{T}(E)_{r_{i}}$ together with the root subgroups  
$\mathbf{G}_a(E)_{x,r_{i}}$ for $a\in \Phi_{i}$ and $\mathbf{G}_b(E)_{x,s_{i}}$ for $b\in \Phi_{i+1}\setminus \Phi_{i}$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Group J(E)^{i+1}_+
nodes.statement:
Similarly, let
$$
\mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}_+ = \langle \mathbf{T}(E)_{r_{i}}, \mathbf{G}_a(E)_{x,r_{i}}, \mathbf{G}_b(E)_{x,s_{i}+} \mid a\in \Phi_{i}, b\in \Phi_{i+1}\setminus \Phi_{i}  \rangle.
$$
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Groups J^{i+1} and J^{i+1}_+
nodes.statement:
These subgroups of $\mathbf{G}^{i+1}(E)$ are invariant under $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ and we set
$\mathsf{J}^{i+1}=\mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}\cap G^{i+1}$, $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ = \mathsf{J}(E)^{i+1}_+\cap G^{i+1}$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Extended character hat phi_i
nodes.statement: The first step is to extend the restriction of $\phi_i$ to $G^i_{x,r_i}$ trivially to a character $\hat\phi_i$ of  $J^{i+1}_+$ \cite[\S4]{Yu2001}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Character phi_i' (case J_+ = J)
nodes.statement:
Next, when $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+=\mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, define a character $\phi_i'$ of $\mathsf{K}^{i+1}$ by 
\begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j),
\end{equation}
for each $k\in \mathsf{K}^i$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Formula for phi_i' (3.1)
nodes.statement: \phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j),
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.label: E:phi'1

nodes.name: Representation phi_i' via Heisenberg-Weil (case J_+ != J)
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, when $\mathsf{J}^{i+1}_+ \neq \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, then instead one uses $\hat\phi_i$ 
 to construct a Heisenberg-Weil representation $\omega$ of $\mathsf{K}^i\ltimes \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$, and then define the representation $\phi_i'$ on $k\in \mathsf{K}^i$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{i+1}$ by
\begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj) = \phi_i(k)\omega(k,j).
\end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Formula for phi_i' (3.2)
nodes.statement: \phi_i'(kj) = \phi_i(k)\omega(k,j).
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.label: E:phi'2

nodes.name: Inducing subgroup K
nodes.statement: Now set $\mathsf{K} = \mathsf{K}^d$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Inflated representations kappa_i
nodes.statement: There is a well-defined inflation process extending each $\phi_i'$ trivially across the remaining subgroups to give a representation of $\mathsf{K}$, which we denote $\kappa_i=\inf_{\mathsf{K}^{i+1}}^{\mathsf{K}}\phi_i'$  \cite[\S3.4]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations

nodes.name: Independence of kappa_i (Hakim-Murnaghan Prop. 3.26)
nodes.statement: Note that this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum \cite[Proposition 3.26]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum

nodes.name: Yu's construction of supercuspidal representations (Theorem 15.1)
nodes.statement: Putting these together, we obtain a representation $\kappa(\Psi)= \kappa_{0}\otimes \cdots \otimes \kappa_{d-1}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that $\pi (\Psi) = \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$ \cite[Theorem 15.1]{Yu2001}.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: $\pi (\Psi) = \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathsf{K}}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(\Psi)=\otimes\kappa_i$ compactly induces to an irreducible supercuspidal $\pi(\Psi)$ of depth $r_{d-1}$.

nodes.name: (K, kappa(Psi)) is a type
nodes.statement: It then follows that $(\mathsf{K},\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.section: 3 The construction of toral supercuspidal representations
conclusions: $(\mathsf{K},\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$

nodes.name: Hakim-Murnaghan equivalence criterion
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data.  Then  $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$.   In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$.
assumptions: $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data
conclusions: $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$
In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$
equivalent_conditions: there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$
nodes.statement_short: Two toral data give equivalent supercuspidals iff their tori are conjugate by $g$ and the products of characters agree on $G^0$ after conjugating.
nodes.label: HMCor

nodes.name: Datum Psi with T = G^0
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ is a toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$ with $T=G^0$.

nodes.name: Twisting character xi
nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be a character of $T$ of depth strictly less than $r_0$.

nodes.name: Proof that Psi_xi is a datum
nodes.statement: The $G^1$-genericity of the character $\phi_0$ of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$ depends only on $\mathrm{Res}_{G^0_{x,r_0}}\phi$.   Since $\xi\phi_0$ and $\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we conclude that $\xi\phi_0$ is also a $G^1$-generic character of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Genericity depends only on the restriction to $G^0_{x,r_0}$, where $\xi\phi_0$ and $\phi_0$ agree.

nodes.name: Twisted datum Psi_xi
nodes.statement:
Thus
$$
\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots, \phi_{d-1}))
$$
is another toral supercuspidal datum.
conclusions: is another toral supercuspidal datum
nodes.statement_short: Twisting $\phi_0$ by $\xi$ gives another toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi_\xi$.

nodes.name: Twisting the datum twists kappa
nodes.statement:
The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that
$$
\kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi).
$$
conclusions:
The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{K}$ such that
$$
\kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi).
$$
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)$ equals $\kappa(\Psi)$ twisted by the inflation $\overline{\xi}$ of $\xi$ to $\mathsf{K}$.
nodes.label: L:Murn

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\mathsf{K}^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$.  Since $\mathsf{K}^1=\mathsf{K}^0\mathsf{J}^1$ and $\mathsf{K}^0\cap \mathsf{J}^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^0}^{\mathsf{K}^1}\xi$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ that is trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \mathsf{K}^0$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$.

Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\mathsf{J}^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\mathsf{K}^0 \ltimes \mathsf{J}^1$  by $\omega$.  
Using now  \eqref{E:phi'1} and \eqref{E:phi'2}, as applicable, to construct $(\xi\phi_0)'$ and $\phi_0'$, we deduce that in both cases $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi' \phi_0'$.

Set $\overline{\xi} = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'$; then  $\inf_{\mathsf{K}^1}^{\mathsf{K}}\xi'\phi_0' = \overline{\xi}\kappa_0$.  Since for $i>0$, $\kappa_i$ depends only on the character $\phi_i$, we conclude that $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of the tensor product to yield $
\kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi),
$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate $\xi$ trivially across $\mathsf{J}^1$, check $(\xi\phi_0)'=\xi'\phi_0'$ from (3.1)/(3.2), then factor $\overline{\xi}$ out of the tensor product.

nodes.name: Inflate $\xi$ to a character $\xi'$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ trivia
nodes.statement: Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\mathsf{K}^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$.  Since $\mathsf{K}^1=\mathsf{K}^0\mathsf{J}^1$ and $\mathsf{K}^0\cap \mathsf{J}^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\mathsf{K}^0}^{\mathsf{K}^1}\xi$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ that is trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \mathsf{K}^0$, $j\in \mathsf{J}^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate $\xi$ to a character $\xi'$ of $\mathsf{K}^1$ trivial on $\mathsf{J}^1$

nodes.statement:
Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\mathsf{J}^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\mathsf{K}^0 \ltimes \mathsf{J}^1$  by $\omega$.

nodes.name: Inequivalence of twisted toral supercuspidals
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum and suppose $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$.  If $\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$,  then $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ and it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial.
assumptions: $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum
$\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$
$\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$
conclusions: $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$
it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial
nodes.statement_short: Twisting $\phi_0$ by a lower-depth character $\xi$ yields a supercuspidal equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ only if $\xi$ is trivial.
nodes.label: P:inequiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$.  In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\mathrm{Res}_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$.   
Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.  
The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$.
Therefore our equality reduces to $\mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) =  \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity.  Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hakim-Murnaghan criterion, then Murnaghan's refactorization results and genericity to force $g\in T$, so $\xi$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Assume equivalence
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$.  In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\mathrm{Res}_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\mathrm{Res}_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume equivalence; Lemma 4.1 gives $g\in N_G(T)$ matching the characters

nodes.name: Refactorization and Murnaghan's Prop 5.4
nodes.statement: Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.
nodes.statement_short: Refactorization and Murnaghan's Prop 5.4

nodes.name: Genericity forces $g\in G^1$
nodes.statement: The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Genericity forces $g\in G^1$

nodes.name: Reduce to depth $r_0$, get $g\in T$, conclude $\xi$ is trivi
nodes.statement: Therefore our equality reduces to $\mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) =  \mathrm{Res}_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity.  Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.

nodes.name: Pointwise stabilizer of a subset of an apartment (Bruhat-Tits)
nodes.statement: Given a subset $\Omega \subseteq {\mathcal{A}}$, the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$ \cite[\S 6.4]{BruhatTits1972}.
assumptions: a subset $\Omega \subseteq {\mathcal{A}}$
conclusions: the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $Z_{\mathrm{b}}$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$

nodes.name: Geodesic [x,y]
nodes.statement: For $x,y\in {\mathcal{A}}$ we write $[x,y]$ for the geodesic from $x$ to $y$; then $G_{[x,y]} = G_x\cap G_y$.

nodes.name: alpha(z - x)
nodes.statement: Given two points $x,z\in {\mathcal{A}}$, we identify $z-x$ with a vector in $X_*(S)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$, and then for each $\alpha \in \Phi$, $\alpha(z-x)$ is a well-defined real number.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad subgroups fix a neighbourhood of x
nodes.statement:
Let ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ be an apartment in $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ containing $x$ and let $\Phi=\Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})$ be the corresponding root system.  Let $s \geq 0$ and define 
$$
\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)=\{ z \in {\mathcal{A}} \mid \forall \alpha \in \Phi, \alpha(z-x) \leq s\}.
$$
Then $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$, where 
$\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$ denotes the simplicial closure of $\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$ in ${\mathcal{A}}$.
assumptions: ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ be an apartment in $\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{G},F)$ containing $x$
$s \geq 0$
conclusions: $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$
nodes.statement_short: $G_{x,s}$ fixes pointwise the region $\Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)$ of points within root-distance $s$ of $x$, and its simplicial closure.
nodes.label: L:stabilizers

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement:
That $G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected.   
Let $z\in \Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$.  For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient.  Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$.  Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.  Since also $Z_s \subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq  G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality from Bruhat-Tits 2.4.13; inclusion by checking each affine root with $\psi(x)\ge s$ is nonnegative on $\Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)$.

nodes.name: Equality of stabilizers by Bruhat-Tits 2.4.13
nodes.statement: That $G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected.
nodes.statement_short: Equality of stabilizers by Bruhat-Tits 2.4.13

nodes.name: Fix $z$ and an affine root $\psi$ with $\psi(x)\ge s$
nodes.statement: Let $z\in \Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)$.  For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $z$ and an affine root $\psi$ with $\psi(x)\ge s$

nodes.name: Show $\psi(z)\ge 0$, so $G_\psi$ fixes $\Omega$
nodes.statement: Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$.  Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\psi(z)\ge 0$, so $G_\psi$ fixes $\Omega$

nodes.name: Conclude using $Z_s\subseteq Z_b$
nodes.statement: Since also $Z_s \subseteq Z_{\mathrm{b}}$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq  G_{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude using $Z_s\subseteq Z_b$

nodes.name: Omega(x,s)
nodes.statement:
More generally, we may define
$$
\Omega(x,s) = \bigcup_{{\mathcal{A}} \ni x} \Omega_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)
$$
which is the union over all apartments of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ containing $x$.

nodes.name: Simplicial closure of Omega(x,s)
nodes.statement: Let $\overline{\Omega(x,s)}$ denote its simplicial closure.

nodes.name: Simplicial radius
nodes.statement:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathcal{B}(G)$ be a bounded convex set and suppose $x\in \Omega$.  For each apartment ${\mathcal{A}} = {\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{S},F)$ containing $x$ define
$$
r(\Omega, {\mathcal{A}}, x) = \sup\{\alpha(z-x) \mid z \in \Omega\cap{\mathcal{A}}, \alpha \in \Phi(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{S})\}.
$$
Then the \emph{simplicial radius} of $\Omega$ with respect to $x$ is defined to be
$$
c(\Omega,x)  = \sup\{r(\Omega, {\mathcal{A}}, x) \mid x \in {\mathcal{A}}\}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Simplicial radius $c(\Omega,x)$: sup over apartments through $x$ of the max of $\alpha(z-x)$ over roots $\alpha$ and $z\in\Omega$.
nodes.label: Def:simplicialradius

nodes.name: Examples of simplicial radius
nodes.statement:
As one motivating example, note that the simplicial radius of $\Omega(x,s)$ with respect to $x$ is $c(\Omega(x,s),x)=s$. For another, letting $\overline{\{x\}}$ denote the simplicial closure of $\{x\}$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$, we have $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$ since 
$\overline{\{x\}}$ is constrained between adjacent affine root hyperplanes in any apartment containing $x$.  Note that in each of these examples we have the equality $c(\Omega,x)=r(\Omega,{\mathcal{A}},x)$ for each apartment ${\mathcal{A}}$ containing $x$.
nodes.statement_short: $c(\Omega(x,s),x)=s$ and $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$.

nodes.name: Simplicial radius of the closure of an optimal point
nodes.statement: One can be slightly more precise about $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)$ when $x$ arises as the point identified with $\mathcal{B}(T)$ from a datum $\Psi$.  In this case, $x$ is an \emph{optimal point} of $\mathcal{B}(G)$, in the sense of \cite[\S6.1]{MoyPrasad1994}, whence the family of such values $c_x=c(\overline{\{x\}}, x)$ could be computed for any $G$.  For example, if $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$, then the optimal points are among the barycentres of the facets, whence if $x$ lies in a $k$-dimensional facet $\mathcal{F}$ then $c_x= 1-\frac1k$.
nodes.statement_short: For $x$ from a datum, $x$ is an optimal point; for $\mathrm{SL}_n$ and $x$ in a $k$-dimensional facet, $c_x=1-1/k$.

nodes.name: Vertex y and G_y
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be a vertex of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ and $G_y$ the corresponding maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.

nodes.name: pi = pi(Psi)
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum with $T=G^0$ and let $\pi = \pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Mackey decomposition
nodes.statement:
Mackey theory gives a decomposition
$$
\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi  \cong \bigoplus_{g \in G_y\backslash G/\mathsf{K}}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa,
$$
where each \emph{Mackey component} $\tau(g):=\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa$ is a finite-dimensional representation of $G_y$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
conclusions:
$$
\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi  \cong \bigoplus_{g \in G_y\backslash G/\mathsf{K}}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y\cap {}^g\mathsf{K}}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa,
$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$ decomposes over double cosets into Mackey components $\tau(g)$.

nodes.name: Mackey components that are types

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.3
nodes.statement:
Let $g\in G_y\backslash G / \mathsf{K}$.  Suppose first that $g^{-1}y \in \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$. Lemma~\ref{L:obvious}, we conclude that $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.

Now suppose that $g^{-1}y \notin \mathcal{B}^T$, so that $T \not\subset G_{g^{-1}y}$.  
Since $s_0>c_T$,  $\Omega(x,s_0)$ contains an open neighbourhood of $\mathcal{B}^T$, so the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$ must meet $\Omega(x,s_0) \setminus \mathcal{B}^T$ in at least one point $z$.  Using now Proposition~\ref{P:line}, we conclude that the corresponding Mackey component contains no types for $\pi(\Psi)$.

Finally, we note that if $\mathcal{B}^T = \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ for a facet $\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{B}(G)$, then since $G$ is semisimple simply connected, each orbit of a vertex $y$ in $\mathcal{B}(G)$ meets $\mathcal{B}^T$ at most once.  By the above arguments, this implies strong unicity.

nodes.statement:
Let $x \in \mathcal{B}(T) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(G)$ and set $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$.  Let  $y\neq y'$ be $G$-conjugate vertices of two distinct alcoves $\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}'$ of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ such that $x \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}\cap \overline{\mathcal{C}'}$.  Then for any $s_0>0$, we have that $y,y' \in \overline{\Omega(x,s_0)}$.  Let $g \in G$ be such that $y'=g^{-1}y$.  If both $y$ and $g^{-1}y$ lie in $\mathcal{B}^T$, then by the proof of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity}, we conclude that both $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ are types for $\pi$ occurring in $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$. Neither are these types isomorphic, since $\pi \cong \textrm{c-}\mathrm{Ind}_{G_y}^G\tau(1)$ implies
$$
\mathbb{C}\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{G}(\pi,\pi) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{G_y}(\tau(1),\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi)
$$
by Frobenius reciprocity.

Let $y$ denote the (non-special) vertex of $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ opposite $\mathcal{F}$, and $w\in G$ a reflection in the wall of ${\mathcal{A}}$ containing $\mathcal{F}$ (viewed as a representative of the corresponding element of the affine Weyl group).  Adopting the convention that a matrix ring stands for its intersection with $\mathrm{Sp}_4(F)$, we compute directly that
\begin{equation} G_{\mathcal{C}} = \bmat{{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} \\ \mathfrak{p}  & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}&{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} \\ \mathfrak{p} &\mathfrak{p} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}&\mathfrak{p}\\ \mathfrak{p}&\mathfrak{p}&{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}&{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}}

{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}  & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} & {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}&{\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}} \\

nodes.name: Fixed points and types in the Sp_4 example
nodes.statement:
In the setting of the preceding example, we can conclude slightly more.  First note that if $z\in {\mathcal{A}}$ and $T\subseteq G_z$, then for each positive long root $\alpha$, we must have $0\leq \alpha(z)\leq 1$.  It follows that ${\mathcal{A}}^T = \overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup\overline{w\mathcal{C}}$, as indicated in Figure~\ref{Fig:1}.  We claim that in fact $\mathcal{B}^T={\mathcal{A}}^T$.

Since $G_x\cap G_y=G_{\mathcal{C}}$, the orbit of $y$ is parametrized by the set $G_x/G_{\mathcal{C}} \simeq \mathrm{GL}_2({\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}})/\mathcal{I}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ denotes its Iwahori subgroup.  A set of representatives is
$$
\left\{\overline{a} = \bmat{1&a&&\\0&1&& \\ && 1&0\\&&-a&1}, w= \bmat{0&1&&\\-1&0&&\\&&0&1\\&&-1&0} \;\;\middle|  \;\;a \in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}/\mathfrak{p} \right\}.
$$
One can verify directly that for each $a \in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}^\times$, ${}^{\overline{a}} T\not\subseteq G_y$.  Thus since the fixed point set $\mathcal{B}^T$ is closed and convex but contains no vertices of chambers adjacent to $x$ outside of ${\mathcal{A}}$, we conclude that $\mathcal{B}^T=\overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup \overline{w\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{A}}^T$, which is contained entirely in the standard apartment.   Therefore we can compute the simplicial radius of $\mathcal{B}^T$ with respect to $x$, yielding $c_T=\frac12$.  

We had see that $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(w)$ gave types.  For $a\in {\scriptstyle{\mathcal{O}}}^\times$, since the choice $z=\overline{a}^{-1}y$ satisfies the hypotheses of  Proposition~\ref{P:line} for any $s_0>0$, we deduce that the corresponding Mackey components $\tau(\overline{a})$ do not contain types.  For the remaining Mackey components, $g^{-1}y$ is not in the closure of an alcove adjacent to $x$, and Theorem~\ref{T:unicity} implies that if $s_0>c_T=\frac12$, any corresponding toral supercuspidal representation contains exactly the two types on $G_y$ identified above.

nodes.name: Sp_{2n} examples with many types
nodes.statement:
Let $n\geq 2$ and consider the subgroup $G' \cong \mathrm{SL}_2(F)^n$ of $G=\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(F)$ generated by the root subgroups corresponding to long roots.  To allow us to be explicit, let the roots of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ with respect to the diagonal torus $\mathbf{S}$ be the set $\Phi=\{\varepsilon_i\pm \varepsilon_j, \pm2\varepsilon_i \mid 1\leq i \neq j \leq n\}$, with simple system $\Delta=\{\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_{i+1}, 2\varepsilon_n\mid 1\leq i < n\}$.   With respect to the basis $\{e_1,\ldots, e_n\}$ of $X_*(\mathbf{S})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$ (whose affine space is ${\mathcal{A}}$), dual to $\{\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n\}$,  the vertices of the fundamental alcove $\mathcal{C}$ are $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^i \frac12e_j$, for $0\leq i \leq n$.  Let $W=W_{\mathbf{G}}$ denote the Weyl group of $\mathbf{G}$ relative to $\mathbf{S}$.


In $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, there are two conjugacy classes of unramified anisotropic tori, attached to the distinct conjugacy classes of vertices in $\mathcal{B}(\mathrm{SL}_2,F)$.  There are between 2 and 4 conjugacy classes of ramified anisotropic tori, attached to the midpoint of facets; see \cite{Nevins2013}, for example.  With respect to the coordinates above, the roots of each $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$ subgroup are $\pm 2\varepsilon_i$, and thus up to conjugacy we can arrange that the vertices have $e_i$-coordinates in $\{0,\frac12\}$, whereas the midpoints have $e_i$-coordinate $\frac14$.

Let each of $T_1,\ldots, T_n$ represent an anisotropic torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2(F)$, ordered so that: for $1\leq i\leq m$, $T_i$ is unramified and attached to $\frac12$; for $m+1\leq i \leq m+\ell$, $T_i$ is ramified and attached to $\frac14$; and for $i>m+\ell$, $T_i$ is again  unramified, but attached to $0$.  Then $T=T_1\times \cdots \times T_n$ embeds as an anisotropic maximal  torus of $G$, and $\{x\} = \mathcal{B}(T)\subseteq \mathcal{B}(G)$ has coordinates
$$
x = \sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j + \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} \frac14e_j.
$$
This is the midpoint of the $1$-dimensional facet $\mathcal{F}$ whose closure is the geodesic $[v_m, v_{m+\ell}]$.  Let $\Omega = \{\sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j +  \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} a_je_j \mid 0\leq a_j \leq \frac12\}$; then $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \Omega$ and one can verify directly that $\Omega = \{z \in {\mathcal{A}} \mid T\subseteq G_z\}={\mathcal{A}}^T$ using the argument of Remark~\ref{R:ex}.  Note that since every maximal facet of $\Omega$ has $x$ in its closure,  $\Omega \subseteq \overline{\Omega_{{\mathcal{A}}}(x,s)}$ for any $s>0$.

Note that $\overline{\mathcal{F}} \neq \Omega$ if and only if $\ell>1$.  In this case, let $W^\Omega = \{ w\in W\mid w\Omega \subseteq \Omega\}$ and let $W_{\Omega} = \{ w\in W\mid \forall z\in \Omega, wz=z \}$.  The elements of $W(T) := W^\Omega/W_{\Omega}$ permute the vertices of $\Omega$.  Let $\mathbf{G}' = \mathrm{Sp}_{2m}\times \mathrm{SL}_2^\ell \times \mathrm{Sp}_{2n-2m-2\ell}\subseteq \mathbf{G}$; then we can identify $W(T)$ with $W_{\mathbf{G}}/W_{\mathbf{G}'}$.  
The vertices of $\Omega\cap \mathcal{C}$ are $v_{m}, \ldots, v_{m+\ell}$.  The vertices $v_m$ and $v_{m+\ell}$ are fixed by each element of $W(T)$, but the orbit of $y=v_{m+t}$ under $W(T)$, for $0<t<\ell$, contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ distinct vertices of $\Omega$.  

Let $\Psi$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$, and $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$.  By the argument of the proof of Lemma~\ref{L:strongunicityfails}, for each vertex $y=v_{m+t}$ with $0<t<\ell$, $\mathrm{Res}_{G_y}\pi$ contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)>1$ inequivalent types.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity
nodes.statement_short: Products of $\mathrm{SL}_2$ tori in $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ give $\binom{\ell}{t}>1$ inequivalent types on $G_y$, growing with rank.
nodes.label: Ex:2

nodes.name: Further classes of tori
nodes.statement: The quadratic tori of Examples~\ref{Ex:1} and \ref{Ex:2} are the smallest of a broad class of tori to which the preceding arguments apply.  For example, using L.~Morris's classification of anisotropic maximal  principal tori of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(F)$ in \cite{Morris1991} one can explicitly construct products of tori of arbitrary rank, obtaining analogous results.  Similar constructive arguments may be made for groups of type $B_n$ and $D_n$.

nodes.name: Hurst's characterization of Coxeter tori
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses that $\mathbf{G}$ is simple, connected and split over $F$ (but not of type $E_7$ or $E_8$), that $T$ splits over a purely tamely ramified cyclic Galois extension, and some mild assumptions on $F$, Hurst proves that $\mathcal{B}^{T_{0+}} = \overline{\{x\}}$ if and only if $T$ is a Coxeter torus (in which case $x$ lies in an alcove) \cite[Satz 13.14]{Hurstthesis}.
